about: Questions an engineer or operator asks of a plant drawing, as data. scripts/question_engine.py runs them over a process model or an extracted twin and writes, for each item a question applies to, the evidence found, the data still needed and where to get it, how the data settles the question, and what a public source says the typical benefit is. A screen, not an audit: it computes no savings for any plant. Rules E1-E26 and C1-C10 follow a research review of public DOE, LBNL, EPA and HSE sources (wording copied from text extracts of those documents); H1-H4 (high-grade heat used for low-grade duty) were added on request and cite the closest source wording, saying so where no number exists. IAC/ITAC statistics are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch, not re-verified against the download; average dollar figures are deliberately left out. See docs/OPPORTUNITY_SCREEN.md.

families.heat_grade: Heat grade (high-grade heat for low-grade duty)

fields_help.applies_when: absent_note: a sentence quoted as evidence saying what was looked for and not found. anchor: a selector (or list of selectors, any may match) for the item that triggers the question. with: clauses that must all find a related item. without: clauses of which none may find one. also_show: related items quoted as evidence if present. group_by: unit | item | model. needs_model: item kinds the model must contain, else the question is reported as not checked. min_anchors: fewest triggering items per group.
fields_help.selector: kind (equipment, instrument, valve = control valve, final_element = other operated valve or speed element, hand_valve, relief, controller, interlock, stream, line_item, offpage), type (exact), type_text (regex over type and text), isa (regex over ISA letters), variable, text (regex over tag, name, description and schedule service), text_all (all regexes), not_text, tagged, control_valve, fact_C_min / fact_C_max (a stated temperature fact), schedule_field (the drawing prints this field, filled or blank).
fields_help.relation: same_unit, same_stream, same_unit_same_medium (same unit and same utility: steam, cooling water, air...), other_unit, discharge_side (streams leaving the anchor's unit; on an extracted twin, within max_hops drawn links on the same sheet, direction unknown), near (same unit or stream; on a twin within max_hops links), drives (a controller writing to the anchor), reads (a controller or interlock reading the anchor), anywhere. twin_only / hand_only: true limits a clause to extracted twins / hand-built models. anchor_kind: the clause applies only to anchors of these kinds.
fields_help.data_requests: item, fields (names looked up in the model's facts and the equipment schedule: present = quoted as evidence; printed but blank = the request names that field on that sheet's schedule; a request stays open while any of its fields is still missing), where (ordered, most direct first: historian (for a role; quantity = flow, temperature, pressure, power, composition or position names only signals that measure it, so a valve position is never offered as a flow; match = a regex the item must match), dcs, nameplate, vendor, maintenance, records, bills, walkdown, or free text), how.
fields_help.typical_benefit: wording copied from the source, source keys, arc = DOE IAC/ITAC recommendation code where mapped. Never a figure for a specific plant.

screen_exclusions.reason: nuclear reactor coolant, chemical and volume control and residual heat removal systems: safety-related design changes go through the licensing basis, not an energy or controls screen

source_notes: S12 is not used (no citable sheet survived review). Figures marked 'as reported in LBNL-56183' come from that report's tables, which quote older secondary sources. Where a source quotes dollar figures they are deliberately not copied: they assume one plant's prices and hours.

questions.question: Is this pump throttled by a control valve when it could run on a variable speed drive?

applies_when.absent_note: no speed control (SC, SIC, SY tag, VFD or VSD) on or next to the pump

also_show.as: other control valve on the discharge

evidence_fields: control valve tag on the discharge

data_requests.item: Control valve position (% open) over normal operation

where.what: read the positioner stroke indicator at several rates

data_requests.how: Take a month or more of valve output at normal sampling; note the typical and the lowest % open, and the hours at each.

data_requests.item: Flow over the same period (a flow-duration curve)
data_requests.how: Bin the flow into ranges and count the hours in each.

where.what: pump curve and rated duty point

data_requests.how: Copy the rated flow and head and get the pump curve.
Copy rated power, speed and efficiency from the motor nameplate.

where.what: elevations and pressures at the suction source and the delivery point
line list or isometrics for pipe lengths and sizes

data_requests.how: Static head = lift plus pressure difference between source and destination; the rest of the pump head at duty is friction plus the valve drop.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a drive quote when the valve normally runs well throttled for long hours and most of the head is friction rather than static lift (VSDs suit friction-dominated systems best). Close it if the valve normally runs near fully open, the head is mostly static, or the pump runs few hours.

typical_benefit.wording: "With rotodynamic pump installations, savings of between 30% and 50% have been achieved in many installations by installing VSDs." Also: "It is estimated that 75% of pump systems are oversized, many by more than 20%."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.4146 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 5,227 recommendations, 3.0 yr average payback, 31.4% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: On a hand-built model the valve sits on a stream leaving the pump. On an extracted drawing the links have no direction, so the rule takes a control valve within four drawn links that do not pass through other equipment; it may still be on a branch or the suction side, so check the drawing. IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is this pump oversized, given a bypass line around it or its valve?
evidence_fields: bypass line or valve near the pump

data_requests.item: Measured flow and head at normal operation

where.what: suction and discharge pressure gauges plus a clamp-on ultrasonic flow meter

data_requests.how: Read flow and suction and discharge pressure at steady operation.
Read BEP flow and head from the curve.

data_requests.item: How often the bypass is open
data_requests.how: Record bypass position over several shifts.

questions.decision_rule: Prioritize the pump if it runs at a flow 30% or more away from BEP or the bypass is used routinely; otherwise close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Five indications: "excessive flow noise, highly throttled flow control valves, heavy use of bypass lines, frequent replacements of bearings and seals, and intermittent pump operation." Prioritize pumps "with flow rates of 30% or more from the BEP flow rates, or with system imbalances greater than 20%." No % saving stated.

questions.limits: A drawn bypass may be normally closed; the drawing cannot show how it is used.

questions.question: Does this pump recirculate flow continuously through a minimum-flow line?
evidence_fields: restriction orifice, MIN FLOW or automatic recirculation valve on a line from discharge back to suction or tank

where.what: clamp-on ultrasonic flow meter on the recirculation line

data_requests.how: Measure both flows at normal operation.
Count hours with recirculation flow.

questions.decision_rule: Worth action when recirculation flows continuously at normal throughput (an orifice that is always open, or a valve that never closes); an automatic valve that only opens at low forward flow is doing its job.

typical_benefit.wording: "the energy needed to push fluid through bypass lines is wasted." No % stated.

questions.limits: Minimum flow protects the pump; never remove it without the pump vendor's minimum continuous flow.

questions.question: Is this motor oversized for its load?
evidence_fields: motor rating field on the drawing (value or blank)

data_requests.how: Copy rated power, full-load amps and efficiency.

data_requests.item: Measured input power or current at normal load

where.what: a clamp-on power meter (or ammeter plus voltage) at the motor starter

data_requests.how: Measure kW (or amps and volts) over a typical period.

questions.decision_rule: Load factor = measured input power divided by (rated output divided by rated efficiency). A motor running well below about 40% of full load is worth a resize question; one oversized slightly is fine.

typical_benefit.wording: "At loads below 40% of full load, motor efficiency begins to decline dramatically." "Slightly oversizing a motor (up to 25%) can actually increase efficiency." No % saving stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.41xx (category only) (IAC/ITAC browse page: motors: 18,002 recommendations, 2.5 yr average payback, 52.3% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: Fires only where the drawing carries a motor rating field (filled or blank); a drawing without one gives no trigger. IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is fan airflow controlled by a damper or inlet vanes instead of speed?

applies_when.absent_note: no speed control on or next to the fan

data_requests.how: Note typical and minimum opening and hours.
Plot the operating point on the fan curve.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a drive quote when the damper normally runs partly closed for long hours; fan power falls with the cube of speed.

typical_benefit.wording: Dampers "remain closed so often that they can be found rusted or locked in a restrictive position... the system continually operates against an unnecessary load." Fan "power is related to the cube of fan speed." No % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.4146 (by description)

questions.question: Is this compressor spilling flow back (recycle or blow-off) more than surge protection needs?
evidence_fields: recycle / spill-back / blow-off valve on it
its controller and power measurement if drawn

data_requests.item: Recycle (or blow-off) valve opening over normal operation
data_requests.how: Take a month or more of valve position; note the hours it is open at normal throughput.

where.what: compressor map with the surge line

data_requests.how: Compare the normal operating point with the surge line plus the controller's margin.
Record power with the valve at its normal opening.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when the recycle or blow-off valve is open at normal throughput, or the controller margin is wider than the vendor map needs. If it only opens during upsets or turndown, close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Blow-off "is a waste of energy and should be used only where necessary to avoid surge." Inlet throttling: "Capacity can typically be reduced from 100 percent capacity to about 70-80 percent with reasonable energy reduction." No % saving stated.

questions.limits: Surge protection is a machine-protection function: any change goes through the compressor vendor and a change review.

questions.question: Does a steam pressure-reducing valve between headers pass enough steam to drive a backpressure turbogenerator instead?
evidence_fields: header text on both sides (HP/MP/LP or pressure rating)

data_requests.item: Steam flow through the station over a year
data_requests.how: "Develop steam flow/duration curves for each PRV station".

where.what: gauges either side of the station

data_requests.how: Record both at normal operation.

questions.decision_rule: Consider a backpressure turbogenerator only if the station passes a constant flow of at least 3,000 lb/hr with a pressure drop of at least 100 psi (S6's condition); otherwise close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Consider when a PRV has "constant steam flows of at least 3,000 pounds per hour (lb/hr), and when the steam pressure drop is at least 100 psi." Installation costs "typically average 75% of equipment costs".

questions.limits: S6 also quotes cost per kW figures; they are deliberately not repeated here. No IAC code maps to turbines (2.2134 covers PRV-station leaks).

questions.question: Is there a steam trap population large enough to justify a trap survey program?
evidence_fields: count and tags of trap symbols

data_requests.item: Trap inventory and last survey date
data_requests.how: Count traps by type and service.

where.what: ultrasonic or thermal survey of each trap

data_requests.how: Classify each trap working / failed open / failed closed.

questions.decision_rule: A survey is likely worthwhile above about 500 traps or when no survey has been done in 3 to 5 years; otherwise fold traps into routine maintenance.

typical_benefit.wording: Unmaintained 3-5 years: "between 15% to 30% of the installed steam traps may have failed." With a program, "less than 5%." LBNL refinery table (as reported in LBNL-56183): trap maintenance 10-15% fuel saved, 0.5 yr payback.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2113 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 445 recommendations, 0.6 yr average payback, 80.1% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is condensate going to drain instead of back to the boiler?
evidence_fields: trap or condensate outlets marked to drain, sewer or grade

data_requests.item: Condensate return percentage and makeup flow

where.what: boiler house makeup and feedwater meters

data_requests.how: Return % = 1 - makeup flow / feedwater flow.

data_requests.item: Contamination risk of each drained stream

where.what: process knowledge of possible leaks into the condensate

data_requests.how: List what could contaminate it.

questions.decision_rule: Worth returning where the drained condensate is clean and the flow is steady; contaminated or tiny streams stay at drain.

typical_benefit.wording: Enthalpy difference "generally over 120 Btu/lb, an amount of energy that is often more than 10% of the energy in the boiler generated steam." LBNL (as reported in LBNL-56183): "Condensate Return Alone 10%", 1.1 yr.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2121 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 354 recommendations, 1.2 yr average payback, 50.9% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is high-pressure condensate flashing to atmosphere when the flash steam could be used?
evidence_fields: flash or vented receiver tag and its vent

data_requests.item: Condensate pressure and flow into the receiver
data_requests.how: Record pressure and estimate flow.
List LP users within reach.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when a steady high-pressure condensate flow vents and a low-pressure user is close by.

typical_benefit.wording: Flash vessels allow "recovery of steam... used in low-pressure steam applications." No % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2127 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 31 recommendations, 1.0 yr average payback, 39.3% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is this hot line insulated?

applies_when.absent_note: no insulation code recorded for the line

evidence_fields: line and its stated temperature or steam service

data_requests.item: Insulation condition and length of bare pipe

where.what: infrared camera or surface thermometer along the line

data_requests.how: Note bare or damaged lengths and their pipe size.
Surfaces over 120 F (49 C) qualify.

questions.decision_rule: Insulate bare lengths over 120 F (49 C) unless they are deliberately bare (for example a line that must cool); closes if the line is already insulated.

typical_benefit.wording: "Insulation can typically reduce energy losses by 90%." "Any surface over 120°F should be insulated." LBNL (as reported in LBNL-56183): insulation 3-13%, 1.1 yr.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2136 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 1,647 recommendations, 2.2 yr average payback, 61.5% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: Many models, and many P&IDs, never record insulation: a finding here means 'not recorded', not 'bare'. IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Are large valves and flanges on hot service left bare?
evidence_fields: valve on a line with a stated hot temperature

data_requests.item: Bare valves and flanges by size

where.what: count bare valves and flanges by size; infrared camera

data_requests.how: Count by size and temperature.

questions.decision_rule: Fit removable jackets on bare hot valves and flanges that are not opened often.

typical_benefit.wording: "a 6-inch gate valve may have more than 6 square feet of surface area." The source tabulates heat saved by valve size and temperature. No % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2136 (by description)

questions.question: Is boiler blowdown manual, with no automatic control or heat recovery?

applies_when.absent_note: no conductivity element or controller near the boiler

where.what: conductivity of boiler water and feedwater

data_requests.how: Blowdown % = feedwater TDS / boiler TDS.

questions.decision_rule: Automate when blowdown is manual and above what the water treatment needs; add heat recovery on steady continuous blowdown.

typical_benefit.wording: "Blowdown rates typically range from 4% to 8% of boiler feedwater flow rate, but can be as high as 10%." LBNL (as reported in LBNL-56183): blowdown heat recovery 1.3%, 1-2.7 yr.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.124x (IAC/ITAC browse page: 334 recommendations, 1.6 yr average payback, 36.7% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Does this boiler stack have no feedwater economizer?

applies_when.absent_note: no economizer anywhere in the model

evidence_fields: no economizer anywhere on the model

where.what: flue gas thermometer at the stack

data_requests.how: Record at normal firing.
Limits how low the flue gas can be cooled.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a quote when stack temperature is high and the fuel allows cooling the flue gas.

typical_benefit.wording: Efficiency "can be increased by 1% for every 40°F reduction in flue gas temperature." An economizer "can often reduce fuel requirements by 5% to 10% and pay for itself in less than 2 years."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.242x (by description) (IAC/ITAC browse page: 635 recommendations, 2.1 yr average payback, 24.3% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Could a condensing economizer serve a cold makeup or process-water heating load?
evidence_fields: cold makeup or process water heating load

data_requests.how: Record at normal firing.

data_requests.item: Size of the low-temperature heat sink
data_requests.how: Flow and temperature rise needed.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a quote when a steady cold water load exists near the stack.

typical_benefit.wording: Can "increase overall heat recovery and steam system efficiency by up to 10%." "Simple paybacks... are often less than 2 years."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.242x (by description)

questions.question: Does this boiler or fired heater run without O2 trim?

applies_when.absent_note: no O2 analyzer near the fired equipment

evidence_fields: no O2 analyzer on the flue

where.what: portable combustion analyzer at several firing rates

data_requests.how: Record O2 and CO across the firing range.

questions.decision_rule: Worth trim when excess air is well above what the burner needs across the firing range.

typical_benefit.wording: LBNL boiler table (as reported in LBNL-56183): "1% improvement for each 15% less excess air."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.12xx / 2.121x (category only) (IAC/ITAC browse page: boilers: 4,622 recommendations, 1.3 yr average payback, 56.5% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Does this furnace or fired heater send hot flue gas straight to the stack?

applies_when.absent_note: no recuperator, air preheater, economizer or waste heat recovery anywhere in the model

evidence_fields: no recuperator, air preheater or load preheat

data_requests.how: Record at normal firing.
Load preheating suits continuous furnaces.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look for continuous furnaces with hot, clean flue gas.

typical_benefit.wording: "Energy consumption can typically be reduced 5% to 30%." Load preheating is "best suited for continuous rather than batch furnaces."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.241x (IAC/ITAC browse page: 1,936 recommendations, 2.0 yr average payback, 20.0% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is heat rejected to cooling water in one place while steam heats a colder stream in another (a heat-integration question)?
evidence_fields: equipment cooled with cooling water and its temperature tags
equipment heated with steam and its temperature tags

data_requests.item: Temperatures and duties of the cooled and the heated streams
data_requests.how: For each stream: supply and target temperature and duty.

data_requests.item: Whether the duties overlap in time

where.what: operating sequence: are both duties needed at the same time?

data_requests.how: Mark each duty continuous, batch or startup-only.
Note pipe run and fouling service.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a pinch or exchanger study only when the hot stream's temperature range sits above the cold stream's with a practical approach, both run at the same time for long hours, and they are close enough to connect. Otherwise close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Pinch potential "far exceeds that from well-known conventional techniques such as heat recovery from boiler flue gas, insulation and steam trap management." No % stated in that section.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.243x; 2.244x (IAC/ITAC browse page: 2.243x: 3,673 recommendations, 1.4 yr average payback, 31.2% implemented; 2.244x: 1,466 recommendations, 1.7 yr, 28.6%; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: A screen pairs any cooling-water-cooled item with any steam-heated item; the temperatures decide. On a reactive system any heat-integration change needs a hazard review first. IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is the compressed air header pressure higher than the end users need?
evidence_fields: air compressor and its pressure control

data_requests.item: Header pressure profile and the minimum end-use pressure

where.what: pressure at the farthest and most demanding users

data_requests.how: Find the highest pressure any user truly needs.

questions.decision_rule: Lower the setpoint toward the highest true end-use need plus distribution losses.

typical_benefit.wording: "for every 2 psi decrease in discharge pressure, energy consumption will decrease by approximately 1 percent at full output flow." With 30-50% unregulated usage, "about 1 to 1.6 percent for every 2 psi."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.4231 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 6,522 recommendations, 0.5 yr average payback, 51.6% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Are compressed air leaks likely, given many quick-disconnects, hose drops or timer drains?
evidence_fields: count of quick-disconnects, hose drops, FRLs, timer drains (proxy evidence only)

where.what: ultrasonic leak survey; a no-load test with production stopped

data_requests.how: Leakage % from load/unload times at no demand.

questions.decision_rule: Run a leak program when leakage is well above the 5-10% target.

typical_benefit.wording: Leaks are "often wasting as much as 20%-30% of the compressor's output"; target "5%-10% of total system flow."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.4236 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 11,223 recommendations, 0.5 yr average payback, 81.4% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is compressed air used for open blowing, sparging, venturi vacuum or cabinet cooling?
evidence_fields: compressed air line to an open-blowing, sparging, venturi or cooling use

where.what: list every air end use and estimate its flow

data_requests.how: Flag uses a blower, pump or fan could do.

questions.decision_rule: Replace inappropriate uses with a blower, vacuum pump or fan where practical.

typical_benefit.wording: "unregulated usage is commonly as high as 30 to 50 percent of air demand."
typical_benefit.arc: 2.4239; 2.4237; 2.4238 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 2.4239: 2,697 recommendations, 1.0 yr average payback, 48.4% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Does the air compressor lack enough storage for intermittent large users?

applies_when.absent_note: no receiver or air storage anywhere in the model

where.what: data-log compressor load and header pressure for a week

data_requests.how: Find short high-demand events.

questions.decision_rule: Add storage when short peaks force an extra compressor on.

typical_benefit.wording: Storage "may allow such a compressor to be turned off." No % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.422x (category only) (IAC/ITAC browse page: 8,589 recommendations, 1.2 yr average payback, 46.5% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is air compressor heat rejected when it could heat something?

data_requests.item: Load hours and a nearby heat sink

where.what: space or water heating needs nearby

data_requests.how: List heat users within reach.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when the compressor runs long hours and a low-temperature heat user is nearby.

typical_benefit.wording: "As much as 80 to 93 percent of the electrical energy" becomes heat; recovery "anywhere from 50 to 90 percent of this".
typical_benefit.arc: 2.243x (by description)

questions.question: Is cooling tower blowdown manual, with no conductivity control or makeup and blowdown metering?

applies_when.absent_note: no conductivity element or controller near the tower

evidence_fields: no flow meter on makeup or blowdown

where.what: conductivity of makeup and tower water

data_requests.how: Cycles = tower conductivity / makeup conductivity.

questions.decision_rule: Raise cycles with a conductivity controller where the water chemistry allows.

typical_benefit.wording: "Increasing cycles from three to six reduces cooling tower make-up water by 20% and cooling tower blowdown by 50%." Recommends a conductivity controller and makeup/blowdown flow meters. No energy % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.2611 (IAC/ITAC browse page: 55 recommendations, 0.9 yr average payback, 45.7% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Is high-grade steam let down, bypassed or desuperheated for a duty a lower grade could serve?
evidence_fields: where the steam comes from and goes to

data_requests.item: Steam flow through the station, with hours
data_requests.how: Build a flow-duration curve: how many hours at each flow.

data_requests.item: Upstream and downstream pressure and temperature

where.what: gauges and thermometers either side of the station

data_requests.how: Record at normal operation.
Copy rated flow.

where.what: operating procedures: startup, trip, normal duty

data_requests.how: Mark the station startup-only, trip-only or normal duty.

questions.decision_rule: If the station passes steam only at startup or trips, close it. If it passes steady flow in normal duty, ask whether a lower-grade source (an extraction or exhaust at the right pressure) could serve the user, or whether the pressure drop could do work: S6's condition for a backpressure turbogenerator is a constant flow of at least 3,000 lb/hr and a drop of at least 100 psi.

typical_benefit.wording: Closest source wording (for the pressure-reducing part, S6): consider a backpressure turbogenerator when a PRV has "constant steam flows of at least 3,000 pounds per hour (lb/hr), and when the steam pressure drop is at least 100 psi." No source found with a number for desuperheater or bypass stations themselves.

questions.limits: Turbine bypass and pegging stations exist for startup, trips and low load; the question is only about hours of normal-duty flow.

questions.question: Is high-grade (or unknown-grade) steam doing a low-temperature job?
evidence_fields: the user's temperature measurement or setpoint
any lower-grade steam on the same sheet

where.what: pressure gauge and thermometer at the supply

data_requests.how: Record supply conditions; saturation temperature follows from pressure.
Note setpoint and normal range.

data_requests.item: A lower-grade heat source on site (a lower steam header, exhaust or waste heat) with spare capacity

where.what: headers and hot streams near this user

data_requests.how: List sources whose temperature exceeds the need with a practical approach.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a change only if a lower-grade source can meet the needed temperature with margin, for the hours the user runs; if the steam is already the lowest grade available, close it.

typical_benefit.wording: Closest source wordings: pinch potential "far exceeds that from well-known conventional techniques such as heat recovery from boiler flue gas, insulation and steam trap management" (S19, no % stated); for letdown to the lower pressure, S6's turbogenerator condition. No source gives a number for matching steam grade to duty.

questions.limits: Where the model does not state the steam grade, the question is first 'what grade is it?'.

questions.question: Is electric resistance heat serving a low-temperature load another heat source could carry?
evidence_fields: electric heater or heat tracing with a stated load temperature at or below 150 C

data_requests.how: Rated kW and run hours.

where.what: hot streams, condensate or cooling water returns within reach

data_requests.how: List sources above the load temperature.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when the heater runs long hours and a lower-grade source above the load temperature is close by.

typical_benefit.wording: No source in the reviewed set gives wording or a number for replacing electric heat with recovered heat.

questions.limits: Fires only when the model states the load temperature; an electric heater with no stated temperature (for example a pressurizer heater) is not a low-temperature load and does not fire.

questions.question: Is heat rejected to cooling water at a temperature another user could use?
evidence_fields: exchanger or user cooled with cooling water
cooling water temperature tags or stated temperatures

data_requests.how: Record at normal operation.
Record at normal operation; the return temperature is the grade of the heat on offer.

data_requests.item: Temperature of the stream being cooled (in and out)
data_requests.how: Record at normal operation.
Duty = flow x heat capacity x temperature rise.

data_requests.item: A heat user that needs heat below the return temperature

where.what: list of heating duties with temperatures

data_requests.how: Match by temperature, hours and distance.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a study only if the heat leaves hotter than a nearby user needs, for overlapping hours; cooling water returning only a few degrees above ambient closes it.

typical_benefit.wording: Closest source wording (S19, pinch): potential "far exceeds that from well-known conventional techniques such as heat recovery from boiler flue gas, insulation and steam trap management." No % stated. For air compressors S11 says recovery "anywhere from 50 to 90 percent" of the heat, which applies to compressors only.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.243x (by description)

questions.limits: Does not fire on equipment that cools the cooling water itself (a cooling water cooler, air-cooled exchanger or cooling tower): that equipment rejects the loop's heat, it does not receive process heat.

questions.question: Is utility use (steam, cooling water, air, fuel, makeup water) metered at this user?

applies_when.absent_note: no flow measurement on the same stream, none on the same user for the same utility, and (on an extracted drawing) no flow element within three drawn links on the same sheet

anchor.text: \bSTEAM\b|COOLING WATER|\bCW[SR]?\b|MAKE-?UP WATER|SERVICE WATER|INSTRUMENT AIR|PLANT AIR|COMPRESSED AIR|NITROGEN|FUEL (GAS|OIL)\b|NATURAL GAS
\bSTEAM\b|COOLING WATER|\bCW[SR]?\b|MAKE-?UP WATER|SERVICE WATER|INSTRUMENT AIR|PLANT AIR|COMPRESSED AIR|NITROGEN|FUEL (GAS|OIL)\b|NATURAL GAS

evidence_fields: utility supply (stream, valve or off-page connector) into a user

where.what: clamp-on ultrasonic flow meter (water) or a vortex/orifice spool piece (steam, air) for a temporary reading

data_requests.how: Measure flow over a representative period and compare with production.
Name the report the meter would feed.

questions.decision_rule: Meter where the user is large enough that its use would change decisions; a meter nobody reads saves nothing.

typical_benefit.wording: "You can't manage what do don't measure" [sic]. Buildings: "efficiency improvements of 10-20%." The guide warns "only success stories are published" and that savings come only if action is taken. LBNL Monitoring & Targeting (as reported in LBNL-56183): "Typical savings 4-17%, average 8%" (UK experience).

questions.limits: On an extracted drawing the check is 'no flow element within three drawn links on this sheet'; the meter may be on the sheet the line comes from.

questions.question: Which measurements have no controller (read by people, or by nothing)?

applies_when.absent_note: no controller in the model or loop list reads these measurements
applies_when.needs_reason: the model holds no controllers; give a loop list with --loops (controller,measurement,output) to check this

evidence_fields: measurement tags not read by any controller in the model or loop list

data_requests.item: Whether operators adjust anything by hand from these readings

where.text: ask the operators which of these they act on, and how often

data_requests.how: Note manual adjustments per shift tied to each reading.

data_requests.item: The control system's own loop list

where.what: export the loop and point list

data_requests.how: Confirm the reading is indication-only and not read by logic the model lacks.

questions.decision_rule: Worth automating a reading that operators adjust by hand often, on a service where steadier control saves energy or quality; indication-only readings nobody acts on close the question.

typical_benefit.wording: "energy and cost savings are around 5% or more for many industrial applications of process control systems" (for plants without updated controls). Process control: "Typically 2-18% savings." The source says these figures "cannot be added".

questions.limits: The model or loop list may be incomplete; an uncontrolled reading may be read by logic not in the model.

questions.question: Do these control valves lack position feedback?

applies_when.absent_note: no position transmitter or indicator (ZT, ZI) drawn on these valves

evidence_fields: control valve tags with no ZT/ZI or positioner feedback drawn

where.what: valve positioner configuration (smart positioner? HART/fieldbus diagnostics?)

data_requests.how: List which valves report position.

where.what: a small step test on each loop in manual

data_requests.how: Compare controller output with measured response.

questions.decision_rule: Add feedback or diagnostics first on valves in energy- or safety-significant loops that show stiction or hunting.

typical_benefit.wording: "Control valve backlash and stiction... are major contributors to process variability." No % stated.

questions.limits: P&IDs often omit positioners; the model saying 'none drawn' does not mean none fitted.

questions.question: Is a control valve bypassed, or oversized for its line?
evidence_fields: globe bypass around it not marked NC/CSC

data_requests.how: Note typical opening.

questions.decision_rule: Resize or trim when the valve normally runs well under half open or the bypass is cracked open.

typical_benefit.wording: "Many control valves normally operate at less than 50% open... a high degree of nonlinearity and thus inconsistent control performance." No % stated.

questions.question: Does the boiler lack O2 trim or three-element drum level control?

data_requests.how: Note O2 trim and level control elements.

questions.decision_rule: Worth an upgrade where O2 trim or feed/steam flow in the level loop is missing on a large boiler.

typical_benefit.wording: LBNL boiler table (as reported in LBNL-56183): "Improved Process Control 3%", 0.6 yr payback.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.121x (category only)

questions.question: Does a temperature controller write straight to a steam valve with no flow controller underneath (a cascade candidate)?

applies_when.absent_note: no flow controller between the temperature controller and the valve
applies_when.needs_reason: the model holds no controllers; give a loop list with --loops to check this

evidence_fields: steam flow measurement if one exists

data_requests.how: Look for oscillation or slow recovery after steam pressure changes.
Note how often supply pressure moves.

questions.decision_rule: A flow slave helps when steam supply pressure swings disturb the temperature; a steady header and a well-behaved loop close it.

typical_benefit.wording: No public numeric source found. Report as qualitative only.

questions.limits: Also covers heating and cooling valves on one exchanger with separate controllers that could fight; that pattern is not detected automatically yet.

questions.question: Do several air compressors run with no master sequencer?

applies_when.absent_note: no sequencer or master controller anywhere in the model

data_requests.how: Look for several compressors part-loaded at once.

questions.decision_rule: Add sequencing when several machines part-load together.

typical_benefit.wording: Control objective "is also to shut off unneeded compressors or delay bringing on additional compressors until needed." No % stated.
typical_benefit.arc: 2.423x (operations, category only) (IAC/ITAC browse page: 20,819 recommendations, 0.5 yr average payback, 67.4% implemented; average dollar figure omitted)

questions.limits: IAC/ITAC figures are browse-page averages read through a summarizing fetch and not re-verified against the downloadable database; averages are skewed by outliers.

questions.question: Are critical steam traps monitored automatically?

data_requests.how: Mark traps whose failure costs most.

questions.decision_rule: Monitor the most important traps online; survey the rest.

typical_benefit.wording: LBNL (as reported in LBNL-56183): "Automatic Steam Trap Monitoring 5%", 1 yr. DOE tip sheet: "Consider online monitoring of the most important steam traps".
typical_benefit.arc: 2.211x (category only)

questions.question: Are there more alarms per operator area than an operator can handle?

data_requests.item: Alarm rate, floods and standing alarms
data_requests.how: Count alarms per 10 minutes in normal operation and after upsets.

questions.decision_rule: Rationalize when the long-term rate or the upset flood exceeds the HSE guidance.

typical_benefit.wording: HSE: "the long-term average alarm rate during normal operation should be no more than one every ten minutes; and no more than ten displayed in the first ten minutes following a major plant upset."

questions.limits: ISA-18.2 / IEC 62682 are not openly accessible; HSE CHIS6 is the citable open alternative.

questions.question: Is a trip or interlock shown for this rotating or fired equipment?

applies_when.absent_note: no safety switch (xSLL, xSHH...), burner management or trip interlock drawn for this equipment

evidence_fields: rotating or fired equipment with no xSLL/xSHH switch, interlock or burner management drawn

where.what: cause-and-effect matrix, HAZOP and LOPA reports

data_requests.how: Confirm what protects each machine and that it is tested.

questions.decision_rule: This is a question to verify, not a finding: close it once the protection is found in the cause-and-effect matrix or safety system.

typical_benefit.wording: Safety benefit; no energy source. Present it as a question to verify, not a finding.

questions.limits: P&IDs often leave trips to the cause-and-effect matrix; 'none drawn' is common and not by itself a gap.

questions.question: Are tank vapors vented to atmosphere with no vapor recovery?

applies_when.absent_note: no vapor recovery or blanket gas anywhere in the model

where.what: vent flow measurement and a gas sample
tank throughput and product vapor pressure

data_requests.how: Estimate vented volume from throughput and breathing.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a VRU study when hydrocarbon vapor volume is steady and large.

typical_benefit.wording: "VRUs can recover over 95 percent of the hydrocarbon..." vapors; "payback in as little as two months" (partner experience).

questions.limits: The source also quotes a partner's annual dollar figure; it is deliberately not repeated.

questions.question: Are relief and vent flows to the flare or atmosphere unmetered?

applies_when.absent_note: no flow measurement on these streams

evidence_fields: streams or reliefs to the flare, vent header or atmosphere
no flow meter or analyzer on them

data_requests.item: Flare or vent flow and composition

where.what: ultrasonic flare-gas meter or a temporary vent flow measurement

data_requests.how: Separate continuous (background) flow from relief events.

questions.decision_rule: Worth metering when background flow is continuous; relief-only lines that seldom lift close the question.

typical_benefit.wording: Background flaring "can be as much as 50% of all flared gases (Miles, 2001)." In refineries it "will generally be less than 50%." No recovery % stated.

questions.limits: Relief paths are safety systems; metering or recovery changes go through a hazard review.
